chunks: Measuring solenoid position. The question: How can you measure the position of a solenoid?
How you measure a solenoid plunger's position depends on what you need to know.
If you only need "home or extended," a limit switch, reed switch, or Hall switch with a small magnet is enough.
For a continuous position you can use a linear Hall sensor, an LVDT (a precise contactless sensor), a sliding potentiometer, or an optical strip.
Or you can use the coil itself, because its inductance rises as the plunger closes the gap.
Think of a trombone. The pitch of a note tells you how far the slide is out.
A solenoid coil works similarly: its inductance, an electrical "pitch," changes as the plunger slides in.
You send a small test pulse and read the response to learn the position, with no extra sensor.
Start from the resolution you need.
In practice most on/off solenoids use a switch; proportional valves use an LVDT; low-cost products try self-sensing first and add a sensor only if accuracy demands it.
Inductance: how strongly a coil resists a change in its current. More iron inside the coil means more inductance, so the current rises more slowly.
Hall switch: a magnetic sensor with an on-off output. A magnet on the plunger triggers it. Linear Hall sensor: gives a voltage that follows the magnetic field.
Its output does not change in a straight line with distance. LVDT: a set of coils around an iron core fixed to the plunger. Its output follows the position, with no contact.
An example solenoid has 48 millihenries of inductance with the plunger open and 170 millihenries when closed.
Apply a 5 volts test pulse for 100 microseconds, short enough that the plunger does not move. The current rises by V t over L . Open, that is 5 times 0. 0001 over 0.
048 equals 10. 4 milliamps. Closed, it is only 2. 9 milliamps. A simple threshold on that current can tell you "closed" without any added part. That is the whole idea.
"For just home or extended, a limit switch, reed or Hall switch.
For continuous position: a linear Hall sensor with a magnet on the plunger (nonlinear, so linearise), an LVDT (precise, contactless, needs excitation), a linear pot, or an optical strip.
Sensorless: inductance depends on air gap, so a small test pulse measures L and hence position, best near the closed end.
I'd pick on resolution, linearity, temperature drift and space."
